overview.title: Matrix–vector and matrix–matrix products
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.section: 2.3 The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations
overview.main_topic: Extending the vector product to a matrix times a vector and a matrix times a matrix, with naive loop implementations, the shape-compatibility rule x.shape[1] == y.shape[0], and the fact that matmul is not symmetric.
overview.central_idea: A matrix–vector product is a stack of vector products (one per row of x); a matrix–matrix product is a grid of vector products (rows of x against columns of y) and is defined only when x.shape[1] == y.shape[0], giving a result of shape (x.shape[0], y.shape[1]).
overview.importance: `matmul(input, W)` in a Dense layer (p.52) is exactly the matrix–matrix product defined here: a batch of input rows against the columns of W. The shape rule on this page is what determines the number of units and parameters of every layer in the book.
learning_objectives: Implement a matrix–vector product with nested loops and explain each assert.
Rewrite the matrix–vector product in terms of naive_vector_product applied to each row.
Explain why matmul is not symmetric once an operand has ndim > 1.
State the compatibility condition and output shape for a matrix–matrix product.
Describe how each coefficient z[i, j] is the vector product of row i of x and column j of y.
prerequisites: naive_vector_product and the dot product of two vectors (p.56)
Matrices as rank-2 tensors with rows and columns (p.46)
Tensor slicing syntax x[i, :] and y[:, j] (p.49)

summary:
The page builds up the tensor product from the vector product of p.56 in two steps.

**Matrix–vector product.** The product of a matrix `x` and a vector `y` returns a vector whose coefficients are the products between `y` and the rows of `x`. The first implementation, `naive_matrix_vector_product`, asserts `x` is rank 2, `y` is rank 1, and `x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]` ("the 1st dimension of x must equal the 0th dimension of y!"). It allocates `z = np.zeros(x.shape[0])` — a vector of zeros with as many entries as `x` has rows — then for every row `i` and column `j` accumulates `x[i, j] * y[j]` into `z[i]`. A second version makes the structure explicit by reusing `naive_vector_product`: `z[i] = naive_vector_product(x[i, :], y)` for each row `i`. This "highlights the relationship between a matrix-vector product and a vector product": the former is just the latter applied once per row.

**Asymmetry.** The authors note that as soon as one operand has `ndim` greater than 1, `matmul` is no longer *symmetric*: `matmul(x, y)` is not the same as `matmul(y, x)`.

**Matrix–matrix product.** The tensor product generalises to tensors with any number of axes, but the most common application is the product of two matrices. `matmul(x, y)` is defined if and only if `x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]`; the result has shape `(x.shape[0], y.shape[1])` and its coefficients are the vector products between the rows of `x` and the columns of `y`. The naive implementation begins on this page: three asserts, `z = np.zeros((x.shape[0], y.shape[1]))`, then a double loop over rows `i` of `x` and columns `j` of `y`, extracting `row_x = x[i, :]` and `column_y = y[:, j]`. The listing is cut off by the page break; the remaining lines (computing `z[i, j]` from `row_x` and `column_y` and returning `z`) are on p.58, where figure 2.5 also visualises the shape rule as a box diagram.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The product of a matrix `x` and a vector `y` is a vector whose coefficients are the (vector) products between `y` and each row of `x`. The nested-loop implementation follows.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Row `i` of `x` is itself a vector of length `x.shape[1]`; dotting it with `y` (which must have the same length) gives one number, `z[i]`. Doing this for all rows yields a vector of length `x.shape[0]`.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is one sample passing through a Dense layer without bias: `W` transposed times an input vector, or equivalently a row of inputs against the columns of `W`. It is also the model of how the full batch product works.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Once either operand has `ndim > 1`, `matmul` is not symmetric: `matmul(x, y)` differs from `matmul(y, x)`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: For two vectors the dot product is symmetric (x·y = y·x). But a matrix–vector product `matmul(x, y)` with `x` of shape `(m, n)` requires `y` of length `n`; swapping the operands would require `y` of length `m`, so `matmul(y, x)` is generally either a different vector or undefined. For matrices, even when both orders are defined the results usually differ.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Operand order matters everywhere in the book: `matmul(input, W)` (p.52) is not `matmul(W, input)`. Getting the order wrong produces a shape error at best and silently wrong numbers at worst.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: for square matrices A and B, AB ≠ BA in general — matrix multiplication is non-commutative.

concepts.name: Matrix product (matmul of two matrices)
concepts.definition: For x of shape (m, n) and y of shape (n, p), matmul(x, y) is the (m, p) matrix whose entry (i, j) is the vector product of row i of x and column j of y. Defined iff x.shape[1] == y.shape[0].
concepts.intuition: Lay every row of x against every column of y; each pairing gives one number; arrange the numbers in a grid with one row per row of x and one column per column of y.
concepts.technical: $z_{ij} = \sum_{k} x_{ik} y_{kj}$. Cost O(m·n·p). Non-commutative. The naive implementation loops over i and j and dots `x[i, :]` with `y[:, j]`.
concepts.significance: It is matmul(input, W) in every Dense layer; the output shape (batch, units) comes directly from (x.shape[0], y.shape[1]).
concepts.misconception: That matmul(x, y) == matmul(y, x). It is not symmetric; often the swapped product is not even defined.

concepts.name: Matrix–vector product
concepts.definition: For x of shape (m, n) and y of shape (n,), matmul(x, y) is the vector of length m whose i-th coefficient is the vector product of row i of x with y.
concepts.intuition: Apply the same vector y to each row of x and collect the m resulting numbers.
concepts.technical: $z_i = \sum_j x_{ij} y_j$. Implemented either with nested loops or as `z[i] = naive_vector_product(x[i, :], y)`.
concepts.significance: The bridge between the scalar-valued vector product and the matrix product; conceptually, one sample through one layer.
concepts.misconception: That the output has length n (the vector's length). It has length m, the number of rows of x.

concepts.name: Tensor product (dot product, matmul)
concepts.definition: Operation that sums products along a shared axis; for vectors it gives a scalar, for a matrix and vector a vector, for two matrices a matrix.
concepts.intuition: Every higher-rank version is a collection of vector products.
concepts.technical: Compatibility: the last axis of x must match the first axis of y (`x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]` for matrices). Not symmetric once ndim > 1.
concepts.significance: Core of the Dense layer and of most of deep learning's linear algebra.
concepts.example: The three naive functions on p.56–57.
concepts.misconception: That it is element-wise. It contracts an axis and changes shape.

math.numerical_example:
$x = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix},\ y = (1, 1)$:

$z_0 = 1\cdot1 + 2\cdot1 = 3$, $z_1 = 3\cdot1 + 4\cdot1 = 7$, so $z = (3, 7)$. Swapping the operands, `matmul(y, x)` = $(1\cdot1 + 1\cdot3,\ 1\cdot2 + 1\cdot4) = (4, 6)$ — different, illustrating the asymmetry.

deeper.title: Reading Dense-layer shapes with the rule on this page
deeper.body:
The first MNIST model (p.41–44) has `Dense(512, activation="relu")` fed by `(batch, 784)` inputs. Inside, `matmul(input, W)` with `W` of shape `(784, 512)`:

- compatibility: `input.shape[1] == W.shape[0]` → 784 == 784 ✓
- output shape: `(input.shape[0], W.shape[1])` → `(batch, 512)`

Then `+ b` with `b` of shape `(512,)` is a broadcast addition (p.55). The second layer `Dense(10)` has `W` of shape `(512, 10)`, giving `(batch, 10)`. Every layer's parameter count (`784·512 + 512`) is readable straight from this shape rule. (The shapes are my worked example; the rule is the book's.)

deeper.title: Why the inner dimensions must match
deeper.body:
1. z[i, j] is defined as the vector product of `row_x = x[i, :]` and `column_y = y[:, j]`.
2. `row_x` has length `x.shape[1]` (number of columns of x).
3. `column_y` has length `y.shape[0]` (number of rows of y).
4. A vector product needs equal lengths (p.56's assert).
5. Hence `x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]` — the 'if and only if' condition.
6. There are `x.shape[0]` choices of row and `y.shape[1]` choices of column, so z has shape `(x.shape[0], y.shape[1])`.

deeper.title: Asymmetry made concrete
deeper.body: With `x` of shape `(3, 2)` and `y` of shape `(2,)`: `matmul(x, y)` is defined (2 == 2) and returns shape `(3,)`. `matmul(y, x)` would need `y`'s single axis (length 2) to match `x.shape[0] = 3` — it fails. For square matrices both orders are defined but differ, as the 2×2 example in formula m2 shows (`[[19, 22], [43, 50]]` versus `[[23, 34], [31, 46]]`). Only the pure vector–vector case is symmetric.

deeper.title: Rows meet columns
deeper.body: Picture x as a stack of horizontal rulers (its rows) and y as a row of vertical rulers (its columns). To fill cell (i, j) of z, pick horizontal ruler i and vertical ruler j, lay them tick-for-tick against each other, multiply matching ticks and add. They must have the same number of ticks — that is the inner-dimension rule — and there is one cell for every (horizontal, vertical) pairing, which is why z is (rows of x) × (columns of y).

misconceptions.claim: matmul(x, y) and matmul(y, x) give the same result.
misconceptions.correction: The page says matmul is no longer symmetric once an operand has ndim > 1; the swapped product is usually different or undefined.

misconceptions.claim: Two matrices can be multiplied whenever they have the same shape.
misconceptions.correction: The condition is x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]; two (3, 2) matrices cannot be multiplied, while (3, 2) and (2, 5) can.

misconceptions.claim: The result of a matrix–vector product has the vector's length.
misconceptions.correction: It has as many entries as x has rows (x.shape[0]); the vector's length is consumed by the dot product.

misconceptions.claim: A matrix product is an element-wise multiplication of corresponding entries.
misconceptions.correction: Each entry of z is a sum of products along the shared axis — a dot product of a row and a column — not a single product.

questions.question: x has shape (4, 3) and y has shape (3, 5). What is the shape of matmul(x, y)?
questions.explanation: x.shape[1] == y.shape[0] (3 == 3) so the product is defined, and the result has shape (x.shape[0], y.shape[1]) = (4, 5). (3, 3) would be the contracted axis; (5, 4) is the shape of y^T x^T, not of x @ y.

questions.question: Compute naive_matrix_vector_product(x, y) for x = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and y = [1, 1]. Then compute matmul(y, x) and comment.
questions.answer: x @ y = [3, 7]; y @ x = [4, 6]. The results differ, showing matmul is not symmetric.
questions.explanation: z[0] = 1·1 + 2·1 = 3, z[1] = 3·1 + 4·1 = 7. For y @ x the entries are 1·1 + 1·3 = 4 and 1·2 + 1·4 = 6. As the page notes, once an operand has ndim > 1 the order matters.

questions.question: In naive_matrix_product, what do row_x = x[i, :] and column_y = y[:, j] represent, and why must they have the same length?
questions.answer: Row i of x and column j of y; z[i, j] is their vector product, which is only defined for equal lengths — hence x.shape[1] == y.shape[0].
questions.explanation: The text says the coefficients are the vector products between the rows of x and the columns of y; the p.56 vector product requires x.shape[0] == y.shape[0] for its two inputs.

questions.question: The second implementation of naive_matrix_vector_product calls naive_vector_product. What relationship does this reveal?
questions.answer: A matrix–vector product is just a vector product repeated for each row of the matrix: z[i] is the dot product of row i with y.
questions.explanation: The page says the rewrite 'highlights the relationship between a matrix-vector product and a vector product'. The inner j loop of the first version is exactly the body of naive_vector_product.

questions.question: Which pair of shapes can NOT be multiplied with matmul(x, y)?
questions.explanation: The rule is x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]. For (3, 2) and (3, 2), 2 ≠ 3, so the product is undefined — same shape is not the criterion. The other pairs satisfy 3 == 3, 5 == 5 and 4 == 4.

questions.question: What does the line z = np.zeros((x.shape[0], y.shape[1])) tell you about the output of a matrix product?
questions.answer: The result has one row per row of x and one column per column of y — shape (x.shape[0], y.shape[1]) — and is filled in entry by entry starting from zeros.
questions.explanation: The callout says it 'returns a matrix of 0s with a specific shape'; that shape is the output shape rule stated in the text.

questions.question: Without looking, write the three asserts of naive_matrix_product and the shape of z. Then explain in one sentence why matmul(input, W) in a Dense layer with input (32, 784) requires W to have 784 rows.
questions.answer: len(x.shape) == 2, len(y.shape) == 2, x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]; z has shape (x.shape[0], y.shape[1]). W needs 784 rows because the compatibility rule requires input.shape[1] (784) to equal W.shape[0].
